title: AI in Arbitration — Promises and Pitfalls — Sir Geoffrey Vos MR, remarks to the BIICL / Jones Day panel, London International Disputes Week (Jones Day offices, London, 4 June 2026)
pub: Judiciary of England and Wales (judiciary.uk) — LIDW panel hosted by BIICL and Jones Day, 21 Tudor St, London
author: Sir Geoffrey Vos

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Vos accepts selective, context-specific deployment but materially extends the cluster by predicting substitution in bounded, consensual arbitration, driven by speed and cost. He also sharpens the governance boundary between party-chosen AI arbitration and compulsory machine adjudication in public courts, while acknowledging current human review and possible failures.
qs: I firmly believe that it is inevitable that AI will eventually be used, not merely to facilitate judicial decision-making, but as the judicial decision-maker in some fields.

It is one thing to impose machine-made decisions on parties to court proceedings, who might justly claim a constitutional right to a decision made by a human judge and even an appeal to a human Court of Appeal.

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: Vos expects AI to make reliable, cheaper and faster decisions, but expressly separates technical capability from legitimate judicial authority. He argues that replacing court judges requires legislative change and raises constitutional and rule-of-law questions, while treating consensual machine arbitration differently because its authority rests on party choice.
qs: So, however, attractive it might be for the parties to a personal injury claim to have their damages assessed in minutes by a capable AI, human judges cannot just be abandoned in the courts without legislative change.

Whilst, as I have said, it is inevitable that the resolution of small disputes at first instance will come to be facilitated by AI, it raises fundamental questions as to the rule of law if we are to deprive humans of final human judicial decisions as to their legal rights.

kp.k: AI decision-making predicted to replace some human adjudication
kp.d: Vos predicts that AI will eventually act as judicial decision-maker in some fields, rather than merely assisting judges. His rationale is anticipated reliability, speed and lower cost, which he expects some commercial parties to prefer. This is a forecast, qualified by his acknowledgment that dispute-specific LLMs still need to be developed and tested for reliability and bias.
qs: I firmly believe that it is inevitable that AI will eventually be used, not merely to facilitate judicial decision-making, but as the judicial decision-maker in some fields.
That is inevitable because AI decisions will be reliable, but cheaper and quicker than human judicial decisions.
the LLMs necessary to make decisions in particular kinds of commercial and other disputes have yet actually be created and tested to ensure their reliability and absence of bias.

kp.k: Court automation faces constitutional and human-rights constraints
kp.d: Vos argues that replacing human judges in courts requires legislation because human judicial decision-making is constitutionally entrenched. He also raises a disputed concern about whether AI can constitute an independent and impartial tribunal under article 6 ECHR. He expects legislative change to take time and provoke disagreement, including over retaining a final appeal to a human judge.
qs: Court services in a democracy cannot just abandon human judicial decision-making in favour of machine-made judicial decisions.
the right to a human judicial decision in crime, civil, family and tribunal cases is deeply entrenched in our constitutional settlement. It would require legislation to change it.
Should, for example, a final appeal to a human judge be retained in every case?

kp.k: Party autonomy supports consensual machine arbitration
kp.d: Vos distinguishes imposed machine adjudication in courts from arbitration chosen by autonomous parties. He argues that parties can agree to final machine determination and considers widespread AI arbitration clauses plausible. As an analogy, he claims some 60 million people annually accept eBay dispute determination within 24 hours, while explicitly expressing doubt—not establishing—that humans determine those disputes.
qs: The parties can engage a human arbitrator or arbitrators or, if they wish, they can agree that their disputes will be finally determined by a machine.
some 60 million people every year are content for their disputes on eBay to be finally determined by eBay within 24 hours, I very much doubt that those disputes are determined by humans.
So, it is by no means far-fetched to envisage widespread AI Arbitration clauses.

kp.k: Reported arbitration deployment retains human review
kp.d: Vos reports that AAA-ICDR announced an AI arbitrator in December 2025 for two party, document-only construction disputes. The reported model assigns merits evaluation and draft-award preparation to AI, while a human arbitrator reviews reasoning and the decision. This is a human-in-the-loop example, not evidence of fully autonomous arbitration.
qs: the AAA-ICDR (the American Arbitration Association – International Centre for Dispute Resolution) (AAA-ICDR) announced in December 2025 that it was offering an AI arbitrator for two party, document-only construction disputes.

It is offering a "human in the loop" model, where the AI arbitrator will evaluate the merits of claims and prepare draft award, but a human arbitrator will review it to test the reasoning and evaluate the decision, in order to quote safeguard trust, transparency and due process.

kp.k: Cost pressures may overcome resistance to autonomous arbitration
kp.d: Vos speculates that human caution is the principal obstacle to wholly machine-made arbitral decisions, but that financial incentives will lead some parties to choose cheaper AI-driven arbitration. He is not unduly concerned about consensual adoption, distinguishing it from imposing machine decisions on court users.
qs: So, what, if anything, is stopping 100% machine-made decisions in the context of arbitration? The answer is probably human circumspection and caution.
parties will probably agree, in some cases at least, to go for the cheapest option, which is likely to be some form of AI-driven arbitration.
It is quite another thing to allow the parties to choose a process that expedites the decision-making to which they have agreed to be bound

kp.k: AI awards may face public-policy challenges
kp.d: Vos regards failures in AI arbitration as inevitable and identifies theoretical legal routes for challenging awards or resisting enforcement. He cites serious irregularity under section 68(2) of the Arbitration Act 1996 and public policy under Article V(2)(b) of the New York Convention, without predicting that such challenges would succeed.
qs: The bigger question, perhaps, is not whether such an AI process should be permitted, but what will happen when it goes wrong, as it surely will.

It would obviously be theoretically possible to try to challenge an arbitration award made in this jurisdiction on the basis that there was a serious irregularity under section 68(2) of the Arbitration Act 1996
or to resist enforcement under the public policy provisions in Article V(2)(b) of the New York Convention.

kp.k: Arbitral overcomplication creates demand for cheaper alternatives
kp.d: Drawing on his experience as an arbitrator before joining the High Court Bench in 2009, Vos argues that arbitral proceedings have become increasingly overcomplicated. He believes this raises party costs and will drive demand for quicker, more cost-effective dispute resolution. This is an experiential assessment rather than a quantified finding.
qs: That is the ever-increasing overcomplication of arbitral proceedings.
This is something I observed when I regularly sat as an arbitrator before coming to the High Court Bench in 2009.

I believe it is something that has increased, I believe it leads to increased costs for the parties and will help drive those same parties to a quicker and more cost-effective dispute resolution mechanism.

kp.k: Digital justice envisaged before formal court proceedings
kp.d: Vos describes promoting an online Digital Justice System through the Online Procedure Rule Committee to resolve civil, family and tribunal disputes efficiently and at minimal cost before court process begins. He recommends applying the same principles at least partly to commercial disputes and predicts AI will enable this transformation.
qs: I am promoting, through the Online Procedure Rule Committee, an online Digital Justice System to resolve all civil, family and tribunal disputes quickly and efficiently, before court process begins, and at minimal cost.
The same principles can and should be applied, at least in part, to commercial dispute resolution, and with the help of AI, they now certainly will.

kp.k: Lawyers face client substitution and urgent adaptation pressures
kp.d: Vos predicts that commercial clients will reject legal services obtainable more cheaply from machines, extending this claim to both advice from ChatGPT, Claude, Harvey or Legora and AI-driven arbitration. He urges rapid professional preparation to retain client trust, while acknowledging an uncertain endpoint and expecting initially slow adoption that may later accelerate.
qs: I am not sure we can now predict accurately where this journey will end, but I am sure that lawyers will need to adapt quickly if they are to retain the trust of their commercial dispute resolution clients.

Businesses will not pay for something they can get more cheaply from a machine. That applies as much to legal advice delivered by ChatGPT, Claude, Harvey or Legora, as it does to AI driven arbitrations.
changes will be slow at first, but when they come, they may accelerate. I believe the legal community needs to prepare itself urgently.

kp.k: Uneven LLM coverage threatens equality and legal sovereignty
kp.d: Vos asserts that US-based LLMs are relevant and comprehensive for the UK but not equivalently suited to multilingual settings in India, Africa and the Global South. He warns against increasing inequalities in global commercial dispute resolution through forfeiting digital and private law sovereignty to dominant LLM home states, notably the US and China.
qs: First, AI and LLMs are not equal across jurisdictions.

We are fortunate here in the UK in that US-based LLMs are, for us, relevant and comprehensive. That is not the case for many multiple language jurisdictions such as India, Africa and the Global South.

AI should not be allowed to introduce greater inequalities into global commercial dispute resolution, caused by the forfeiture of digital and private law sovereignty to the dominant home states of LLMs such as the US and China.

kp.k: Final human adjudication carries distinct rule-of-law significance
kp.d: Vos distinguishes last-resort judicial decisions from government decisions affecting rights and consensual arbitral determinations. While predicting AI facilitation of small disputes at first instance, he argues that removing final human judicial decisions raises fundamental rule-of-law questions.
qs: Judicial decision-making is the last resort.

Whilst, as I have said, it is inevitable that the resolution of small disputes at first instance will come to be facilitated by AI, it raises fundamental questions as to the rule of law if we are to deprive humans of final human judicial decisions as to their legal rights.

kp.k: Machine speed does not ensure rapid human acceptance
kp.d: Vos cautions that rapid AI processing and decision-making cannot eliminate the time people need to accept adverse outcomes. He contrasts decisions produced in seconds with human adjustment over days or months, warning against expecting acceptance to match technical speed.
qs: AI can make decisions and process data in seconds.
And humans take days or months to process and reach acceptance of unwelcome outcomes.
If AI reaches decisions affecting humans and their businesses super-quickly, we should not expect those outcomes to be accepted in the same time-frame.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Vos predicts that AI will eventually make judicial decisions in some fields, rather than merely assist judges, because he expects reliable AI decisions to be cheaper and quicker.
pts.d: Sir Geoffrey Vos presents substitution for human decision-makers as inevitable in some fields, not across all judicial work. His anticipated commercial demand rests on comparable reliability combined with immediate decisions at substantially lower cost. He also predicts AI facilitation of first-instance small disputes, while distinguishing that from removing access to a final human judicial decision.

pts.k: Vos anticipates consensual AI arbitration, with cost pressures encouraging some parties to choose machine-made awards.
pts.d: Vos contrasts autonomous commercial parties choosing arbitration procedures with courts imposing machine decisions. He considers widespread AI arbitration clauses plausible and expects the cost and complexity of conventional arbitration to drive demand for alternatives. He distinguishes fully machine-made awards from the human-reviewed AAA-ICDR model he describes.

pts.k: Vos predicts substantial changes to dispute resolution and competitive pressure on lawyers from cheaper machine-provided advice and arbitration.
pts.d: Vos links AI to his proposed online Digital Justice System for resolving civil, family and tribunal disputes before court proceedings, and predicts application of similar principles to commercial disputes. He argues that lawyers must adapt rapidly to retain commercial clients' trust because businesses will not pay for services available more cheaply from machines. ChatGPT, Claude, Harvey and Legora are named as sources of AI-delivered legal advice; he provides no comparative product-performance evidence.

pts.k: Vos expects failures, uneven jurisdictional benefits and a gap between AI decision speed and human acceptance.
pts.d: Vos states that AI arbitration will sometimes go wrong and identifies possible public-policy challenges to awards or enforcement, without predicting their success. He says LLM relevance and comprehensiveness vary across jurisdictions and warns against increased global inequalities and loss of digital and private-law sovereignty. He also argues that rapid decisions will not produce equally rapid acceptance by affected people and businesses.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Vos supports the arbitration outlook with a reported service announcement, an eBay analogy and his own arbitration experience; he supplies no measured reliability or cost comparisons.
pts.d: Vos reports that AAA-ICDR announced an AI arbitrator in December 2025 for two-party, document-only construction disputes. As described, AI evaluates claims and drafts an award, while a human arbitrator checks the reasoning and decision: this is human-reviewed assistance, not evidence of fully autonomous awards. Vos cites approximately 60 million people annually accepting eBay dispute determinations within 24 hours, but explicitly presents the absence of human decision-makers as his inference. His claim about overcomplication draws on experience as an arbitrator before joining the High Court in 2009; its subsequent increase is stated as a belief. Predictions of future reliability, lower costs and uptake are not supported by benchmarks or comparative studies in the speech.

pts.k: Legal constraints and possible challenge routes are grounded in cited legal provisions and Vos's constitutional interpretation, rather than reported AI-award litigation.
pts.d: Vos cites Article 6 ECHR, the constitutional position of human judicial decision-making, section 68(2) of the Arbitration Act 1996 and Article V(2)(b) of the New York Convention. His Article 6 interpretation is expressly disputed and the supplied script contains an internally garbled formulation of it; the clearer accompanying claim is that abandoning human judges requires legislation. Award challenges are presented as theoretical possibilities. His digital-justice initiative supplies institutional context, not evidence of achieved AI outcomes. No empirical basis is supplied for the jurisdictional comparison or human-acceptance times.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The June 2026 speech predicts eventual transformation without a fixed deadline; initial adoption is expected to be slow and potentially accelerate.
pts.d: Vos acknowledges uncertainty about the ultimate destination. Court substitution depends on legislative change, contested constitutional choices and creation and testing of suitable models for reliability and absence of bias. Arbitration is presented as more immediately open to party agreement, although fully machine-determined disputes are not yet commonplace. Uptake is qualified as occurring in some cases and is conditioned on caution, cost advantages and party consent. The reported December 2025 AAA-ICDR offering has a narrow dispute scope and retains human review.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Commercial parties, lawyers, arbitrators and court users face different combinations of cost savings, substitution pressure and safeguards.
pts.d: Commercial clients are the principal predicted adopters of cheaper AI advice and consensual arbitration. Lawyers face pressure to adapt and maintain trust; human arbitrators may review AI drafts or, in the fully automated scenario, be replaced as decision-makers. Parties to the reported AAA-ICDR construction process receive human-reviewed AI assistance. Civil, family and tribunal users are the intended beneficiaries of Vos's proposed pre-court digital system. People in criminal and other court proceedings retain a distinct constitutional interest in human adjudication, and personal-injury claimants illustrate both potential speed gains and legislative constraints.

pts.k: Vos identifies unequal exposure across jurisdictions and warns that individuals and businesses still need time to accept adverse outcomes.
pts.d: Vos regards the UK as relatively well served by US-based LLMs, contrasting it with multilingual settings in India, Africa and the Global South. He warns of inequality and sovereignty risks where dominant models originate in the US and China. Separately, people and businesses subject to rapid decisions may take days or months to accept them; removing final human judicial decisions raises rule-of-law concerns for rights holders.
